Bluetooth Low Energy, from the radio up · Start here · 1 of 5

A year on a coin battery

A heart-rate strap runs for months on a battery the size of a coin. Here's the one idea that makes that possible, and that every later puzzle follows from.

The problem

Your Bluetooth headphones need charging every day or two. A heart-rate strap, a key finder or a plant sensor runs for months on a battery the size of a coin. Both talk over Bluetooth. What do the small devices do differently?

See it

Save this diagram as a GIF

The building block

A device's radio is the part that sends and listens over the air. A radio that is on, sending or just listening, uses far more power than the rest of the device asleep. For a small device, it's the hungriest part.

Bluetooth Low Energy, BLE for short, is the kind of Bluetooth built for tiny batteries. Its trick is simple to say: keep the radio off almost all the time. The device sleeps, wakes for a few milliseconds to send or listen, and goes back to sleep for much longer than it was awake: anything from a few milliseconds (ms) to seconds. Your headphones use the original Bluetooth, which keeps the radio busy streaming sound; that's why they need charging every day or two.

That creates the two problems the next puzzles solve. A device that's asleep almost all the time is hard to find: how does your phone ever hear it? (puzzle 1) And once they've found each other, how do two devices that both sleep meet at the same moment? (puzzle 2)

The analogy

A lighthouse keeper on a tiny budget. Leaving the lamp on all night empties the fuel tank. So the keeper flashes it for a split second, then waits, then flashes again. Ships learn to watch for the flashes.

Check yourself

A strap's battery is nearly empty after two days instead of months. What's the most likely cause?

Not quite. Any coin battery would drain like that; what decides it is how long the radio is awake.

Not quite. BLE is built for coin-sized batteries: the size isn't the problem, how long the radio is on is.

Right. Battery life is decided by how much of the time the radio is on.

Why does BLE save power by sleeping, instead of by sending less data?

Right. Being on, even just listening, is the cost; sleeping is the saving.

Not quite. Sleeping doesn't change the messages; it changes how long the radio is on. Re-read that part ↑

What's the difference between BLE and the Bluetooth in your headphones?

Not quite. They share the name and the airwaves, but BLE's whole design is about keeping the radio off.

Right. Same airwaves, different goal: BLE optimizes for battery, not for streaming.

Sources

  • Bluetooth Core Specification 5.4, Vol 6, Part B: Link Layer (devices meet at planned moments: "A connection event is a point of synchronization between the Central and the Peripheral")

What you now know

The radio is the hungriest part of a small device. BLE keeps it off almost all the time and wakes it only for short, planned moments. Every rule in this course follows from that.
